subtopic_detail: Persistent yearning thirteen months after a spouse died with preserved capacity for pleasure
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 68 year old woman whose husband died of bowel cancer thirteen months ago. She has come in for a routine appointment and, when asked how she is coping, says she thinks about him for most of the day and still keeps his voicemail greeting on her phone so that she can hear his voice.

She has not entered his study since the funeral and has turned down two invitations from her walking group because going without him feels like a betrayal. She sleeps about five hours a night and has lost 3 kg. She still looks forward to her granddaughter's Saturday swimming lessons and enjoys them when she is there, and she does not feel that she has failed anyone or that she is a burden. She has no thoughts of harming herself, although she says she would not mind if she did not wake up one morning.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when speaking about her husband, affect reactive to other topics, no psychomotor retardation, Mini-Mental State Examination 29 out of 30
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start sertraline 50 mg daily with weekly phone review and reassess at four weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressant monotherapy targets a depressive episode, and the cognitive features that define one are absent here: her affect is reactive, she retains anticipatory pleasure, and she has no worthlessness or guilt. Antidepressants treat a comorbid depressive episode when present but do not reduce grief severity on their own. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Refer for grief focused cognitive behavioural therapy and reassess at four weeks
options.rationale: Intense daily yearning, preoccupation, avoidance of reminders and an inability to re-engage with previously valued activities, persisting beyond twelve months from the death and causing functional impairment, define a grief specific disorder rather than an ordinary bereavement reaction. Structured grief focused psychotherapy that combines exposure to the avoided reminders with restoration of goals has the strongest evidence for this presentation. (Source: Australian Centre for Grief and Bereavement: Prolonged grief disorder practice guidance)
source_refs: Australian Centre for Grief and Bereavement: Prolonged grief disorder practice guidance

options.text: Refer for eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing and reassess at four weeks
options.rationale: This is a trauma memory processing therapy, and the intrusions she describes are longing and yearning rather than the re-experiencing of a horrifying event. The distinction from the correct answer is the content of the intrusions: reprocessing therapies are indicated when the death itself was witnessed as traumatic and is being relived with fear. (Source: Australian Centre for Grief and Bereavement: Prolonged grief disorder practice guidance)
source_refs: Australian Centre for Grief and Bereavement: Prolonged grief disorder practice guidance

options.text: Advise that this is within the expected range and reassess her at four weeks
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is correct in the first six to twelve months, when avoidance and yearning of this intensity are normative and self limiting. Past twelve months with persisting impairment the probability of spontaneous resolution falls sharply, and continued observation simply delays effective treatment. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start mirtazapine 15 mg at night with weekly phone review and reassess at four weeks
options.rationale: Mirtazapine is chosen for a depressive episode with insomnia and weight loss, and both are present, but they sit inside a grief specific picture without the defining cognitive features. Sedating antidepressants also add falls and daytime sedation risk in this age group while leaving the avoidance that maintains the disorder untouched. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Grief becomes a disorder when the intensity and the avoidance persist long enough to block re-engagement with life, and the Australian diagnostic threshold in adults is a death at least twelve months earlier. The separation distress features are yearning, preoccupation with the deceased, identity disruption, avoidance of reminders, emotional numbness and a sense that life is meaningless. The trap in general practice is to read weight loss and broken sleep as a depressive episode and prescribe, because the physical symptoms overlap almost completely; the discriminators are pervasive anhedonia, worthlessness and guilt, all of which are preserved or absent in uncomplicated grief. Risk factors include a sudden or violent death, the loss of a child or spouse, social isolation and high dependency on the deceased. Untreated, the disorder carries elevated rates of cardiac events, alcohol misuse and suicide, so identifying it matters more than the label suggests.
key_points: The adult diagnostic threshold is at least twelve months since the death with persisting impairment
Reactive affect, preserved anticipatory pleasure and absent worthlessness separate grief from a depressive episode
Grief focused psychotherapy with exposure to avoided reminders is first line
Antidepressants treat a comorbid depressive episode, not the grief itself
Passive wishes to be with the deceased still warrant an explicit suicide risk assessment
explanation.pearls: In the randomised trial that tested the two together, adding citalopram 20 mg daily to grief focused psychotherapy did not reduce grief severity beyond the psychotherapy alone, although it did improve co-occurring depressive symptoms, which is the practical reason to lead with therapy and reserve the antidepressant for a clear comorbid episode.

sources.label: Australian Centre for Grief and Bereavement: Prolonged grief disorder practice guidance
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Sleep attacks with knee buckling during laughter in a student referred as treatment resistant low mood
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 19 year old engineering student referred with low mood that has not responded to two antidepressants at adequate dose and duration. He describes being exhausted all day, falling asleep in lectures and once while eating dinner, despite sleeping nine hours overnight.

His mood lifts when he is with friends and he still enjoys gaming and football, and there has been no change in appetite or weight. He mentions, when asked what happens when he laughs hard, that his knees buckle and his jaw sags for about twenty seconds while he stays fully aware of what is going on around him. As he is falling asleep he sometimes sees people in the room who are not there. He drives forty minutes each way to campus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, no tonsillar hypertrophy, neurological examination normal, Epworth Sleepiness Scale 19 out of 24
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), ferritin 88 micrograms/L (30-300), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Switch to a noradrenergic antidepressant and review his energy in four weeks
options.rationale: A third antidepressant assumes the diagnosis is a depressive episode, but his affect is reactive, his interests are intact and his appetite and weight are unchanged, so the two failed trials are better explained by the wrong target than by treatment resistance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Start modafinil 100 mg each morning and review his daytime sleepiness in four weeks
options.rationale: Modafinil is a reasonable eventual treatment for the sleepiness but prescribing it before objective testing removes the evidence the diagnosis depends on, because stimulants and wake promoting agents must be withheld before the sleep latency study. It also leaves the episodic weakness untreated. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management

options.text: Arrange overnight oximetry and refer for consideration of continuous positive airway pressure
options.rationale: Obstructive sleep apnoea is the common cause of excessive daytime sleepiness, but he has a body mass index of 23 kg/m2, no snoring history and no witnessed apnoeas, and oximetry alone would miss the sleep onset abnormality being looked for. Airway pressure therapy does not address sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management

options.text: Refer for overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
options.rationale: Sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter with retained awareness, together with hypnagogic hallucinations and irresistible daytime sleep despite adequate night sleep, is the pattern that requires objective sleep testing. Overnight study excludes another sleep disorder first, and the daytime latency study then measures mean sleep latency and sleep onset rapid eye movement periods, which is what confirms the diagnosis. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia and a two week sleep diary
options.rationale: This therapy targets difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep with insufficient sleep opportunity, and he sleeps nine hours without difficulty, so there is no sleep restriction to correct. A diary alone will document the daytime sleep attacks without ever explaining the episodic weakness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy is frequently misdiagnosed as depression for years because excessive daytime sleepiness, poor concentration and social withdrawal read as depressive symptoms at first pass, and because the age of onset in the teens and twenties coincides with the peak incidence of mood disorders. The feature that separates them is cataplexy, a sudden partial or complete loss of skeletal muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, most often laughter, with consciousness fully preserved throughout. The full tetrad adds sleep paralysis and hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations, but fewer than a third of patients report all four. Diagnosis requires overnight polysomnography to exclude another cause of disrupted sleep, followed the next day by a multiple sleep latency test showing a mean sleep latency of eight minutes or less with two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods. Type 1 disease reflects loss of hypothalamic orexin producing neurons and can be confirmed on cerebrospinal fluid orexin when the clinical picture is ambiguous.
key_points: Cataplexy is emotion triggered loss of muscle tone with fully preserved awareness
Sleepiness despite adequate overnight sleep argues against a depressive episode
Overnight polysomnography must precede the multiple sleep latency test
Wake promoting drugs and stimulants must be withheld before the latency study
Reactive affect and intact interests are the clinical discriminators from depression
explanation.pearls: Advise him not to drive until the sleepiness is controlled and report the condition as required: the Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive standard treats untreated narcolepsy with excessive daytime sleepiness as incompatible with a private licence, and a conditional licence normally requires at least three months of demonstrated symptom control with specialist review.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management

subtopic_detail: Hair pulling with a patch of scalp thinning and relief on pulling in a university student
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 20 year old woman who has noticed a thinning patch at the right crown of her scalp over the past six months. She admits, once asked directly, that she pulls hairs out one at a time while reading and while watching television, mostly in the evenings.

She describes a mounting tension before she pulls and a settling of that tension afterwards, and she has tried to stop several times without success. She does not believe anything is living in her scalp, has no checking, washing or ordering rituals, and does not examine her appearance repeatedly in mirrors. She is embarrassed enough to part her hair differently but has not withdrawn from friends or study.

data_table.Examination: A 4 cm patch of reduced hair density at the right crown containing hairs of many different lengths, no scaling, no erythema, no scarring, no broken hairs elsewhere, eyebrows and eyelashes intact
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 64 micrograms/L (30-300), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Refer for habit reversal training and review her scalp in eight weeks
options.rationale: Recurrent pulling with rising tension beforehand and relief afterwards, repeated unsuccessful attempts to stop, and visible hair loss define a body focused repetitive behaviour, and behavioural therapy built on awareness training plus a competing response is the treatment with the best evidence and the lowest harm. Review at eight weeks allows an objective look at regrowth in the patch. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Start fluoxetine 20 mg daily and review her scalp in eight weeks
options.rationale: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are effective for obsessive compulsive disorder but have repeatedly failed to beat placebo for pulling behaviours, which is the key difference between the two conditions despite their being grouped together. She also has none of the intrusive thoughts or neutralising rituals that would justify the trial. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Start N acetylcysteine 1200 mg twice daily and review her scalp in eight weeks
options.rationale: This glutamate modulator has modest trial support in adults and is a reasonable second line option, but it is an adjunct rather than the initial step and has not outperformed behavioural therapy. Starting it first also forgoes the skills that prevent relapse once any drug is stopped. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Refer to a dermatologist for scalp biopsy and review the result in eight weeks
options.rationale: Biopsy is used when the cause of patchy hair loss is uncertain, and here it is not: hairs of varying length within the patch with no scaling and no scarring is the described appearance of self inflicted pulling, unlike the smooth patch with tapered exclamation mark hairs of alopecia areata or the scaling and broken hairs of a fungal infection. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists

options.text: Start olanzapine 2.5 mg at night and review her scalp in eight weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are considered only in refractory cases and carry metabolic and weight consequences that are hard to justify in a well young woman with a localised behaviour. There is no delusional belief about infestation here that would place this on a psychotic spectrum. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Trichotillomania sits in the obsessive compulsive and related disorders chapter but behaves quite differently from obsessive compulsive disorder in treatment response, which is the practical point for an exam. Pulling is typically automatic during sedentary focused activity rather than driven by an intrusive fear, and there is no neutralising ritual, so serotonin reuptake inhibitors have little effect. Habit reversal training teaches the patient to detect the pulling early, substitute an incompatible motor response such as clenching a fist for a minute, and modify the environment that cues the behaviour. Trichophagia, the swallowing of pulled hair, must be asked about because a retained hair mass can present later as gastric outlet obstruction. Comorbid depression, anxiety and excoriation disorder are common and change the management plan if present.
key_points: Rising tension before pulling and relief afterwards is the defining phenomenology
Hairs of varying length within the patch without scaling or scarring is the visual sign
Habit reversal training is first line and outperforms serotonin reuptake inhibitors
N acetylcysteine is a reasonable second line adjunct in adults
Always ask about swallowing the hair because of the risk of a gastric hair mass
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether she swallows the hair, because a trichobezoar can extend through the pylorus into the small bowel as Rapunzel syndrome and is the one complication of this disorder that becomes a surgical emergency, typically presenting with early satiety and vomiting years after the pulling began.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Parents seeking clinical information after an adult son with first episode psychosis refuses consent to share
stem:
You are the registrar in an early psychosis service caring for a 21 year old man who is three weeks into treatment for a first episode of psychosis. He is a voluntary patient, his persecutory beliefs have receded, and a formal assessment two days ago found him able to understand, retain, weigh and communicate decisions about his care. He has asked the team in writing not to discuss anything about him with his parents, with whom he lives.

His mother telephones you. She does the shopping, prompts him about his tablets each evening and drives him to appointments. She asks what is wrong with him, what the tablets are and what she should be watching for, and adds that she found a syringe in the bathroom bin this morning.

data_table.Examination: Settled in manner, no thought disorder, no current delusional beliefs elicited, no extrapyramidal signs, insight partial
data_table.Investigations: Capacity assessment documented as intact two days ago, urine drug screen at admission positive for cannabis only, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to the mother?

options.text: Decline any contact with her until her son provides written consent to share information
options.rationale: Refusing to take the call confuses two separate duties: disclosure is restricted by his refusal, but receiving information from a family member never requires his consent and is often the only route by which a safety concern reaches the team. Declining contact also alienates the carer who supports adherence. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Partnering with carers position statement)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Partnering with carers position statement

options.text: Confirm his diagnosis and medication to her because she is his main practical carer
options.rationale: Being the practical carer does not create a right of access to the clinical record of an adult with capacity, and disclosure against an explicit written refusal breaches privacy law and typically destroys the therapeutic relationship at the point where adherence is most fragile. (Source: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner: Australian Privacy Principles)
source_refs: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner: Australian Privacy Principles

options.text: Listen to her concerns, and give general information about psychosis and carer supports
options.rationale: Information can always flow towards the clinician, so her account of the syringe is received and acted on, and generic education about the illness, about medication side effects in general terms and about carer support services discloses nothing specific to him. The syringe is then explored directly with him as a clinical matter, which is also the conversation most likely to earn his consent to include her. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Partnering with carers position statement)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Partnering with carers position statement

options.text: Ask him again next week and telephone her with an answer once he has decided
options.rationale: Revisiting consent is right, but deferring the whole conversation for a week leaves an unexplored report of injecting drug use sitting with the family rather than with the treating team. The timing, not the principle, is what makes this wrong. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Partnering with carers position statement)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Partnering with carers position statement

options.text: Invite her to a family meeting and set out his treatment plan there without asking him
options.rationale: A family meeting is an excellent intervention in first episode psychosis and reduces relapse, but convening one to disclose his plan without revisiting his refusal is the same breach as a telephone disclosure with more people in the room. It becomes the right answer once he consents. (Source: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner: Australian Privacy Principles)
source_refs: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner: Australian Privacy Principles

explanation.summary: Carer involvement in first episode psychosis improves adherence and reduces relapse, so the reflex to shut families out on privacy grounds causes real clinical harm. The resolution taught in Australian services is directional: information flowing from the carer to the team requires no consent at all, while information flowing from the team to the carer requires the consent of an adult with capacity. Generic information about the illness, about treatment options and about carer support services is not personal information and can always be given. Consent is not a single event, and a patient who refuses in week three often agrees in week eight once trust is established, so it is revisited at each review and the reasons for refusal are explored rather than accepted at face value. The exceptions that permit disclosure without consent are narrow: a serious and imminent threat to the life, health or safety of the patient or another person, or where the patient lacks capacity and disclosure is in their best interests.
key_points: Receiving information from a carer never requires the patient's consent
Disclosure to a carer requires consent from an adult with capacity
Generic illness and carer support information is not personal information
Consent is revisited at every review, not treated as a final answer
Disclosure without consent requires a serious and imminent threat or absent capacity
explanation.pearls: A carer reporting drug paraphernalia in first episode psychosis is clinically urgent rather than merely a privacy problem: continued substance use roughly doubles the two year relapse rate in this group, and an injecting route also changes the screening you order, so the conversation with him about it happens the same day rather than at the next scheduled review.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Partnering with carers position statement
Office of the Australian Information Commissioner: Australian Privacy Principles
Orygen: Australian clinical guidelines for early psychosis

subtopic_detail: Choosing the delivery mode of psychological treatment for moderate depression in a fly in fly out worker
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 41 year old man who works a two weeks on, one week off roster at an iron ore mine in the Pilbara and flies home to Perth for his week off. For three months he has had low mood most days, poor concentration at work and early waking, with a Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score of 15.

He drinks six standard drinks on two or three nights during his week at home and none on site. He has no thoughts of self harm, no history of elevated mood, and no psychotic features. He tells you his brother had a bad time coming off an antidepressant and that he does not want tablets. His camp has reliable internet in the donga and a quiet room he can use after shift.

data_table.Examination: Reduced spontaneous speech, restricted affect, no psychomotor retardation, no cognitive deficit on bedside testing
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), gamma glutamyl transferase 38 units/L (less than 60), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prepare a mental health treatment plan and refer for video delivered cognitive behavioural therapy
options.rationale: Structured psychological therapy is the appropriate first treatment for moderate severity depression in a patient who declines medication, and the roster is what decides the delivery mode: weekly sessions cannot be sustained face to face when he is away for two weeks in three, whereas video sessions from the camp preserve the weekly spacing that the therapy depends on. A mental health treatment plan is what unlocks the subsidised sessions. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners

options.text: Prepare a mental health treatment plan and refer for face to face sessions during his weeks at home
options.rationale: This is the default referral and fails on scheduling rather than on principle: sessions three weeks apart fall well outside the weekly to fortnightly spacing at which this therapy has been shown to work, and the between session tasks lose their momentum. It becomes correct if he moves to a residential role. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners

options.text: Recommend a self guided internet program and review his symptom score in twelve weeks
options.rationale: Unguided digital programs are an evidence based option for mild depression, but completion rates fall sharply and effect sizes shrink at moderate severity, and a score of 15 with functional impairment at work sits above the band where a self guided program is sufficient on its own. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Recommend a structured exercise program and review his symptom score in twelve weeks
options.rationale: Exercise is a genuine adjunct with a small to moderate effect and should be encouraged alongside treatment, but as the sole intervention for moderate depression it leaves the condition undertreated for three months. Recommending it alone also risks reading as dismissal to a patient who has just disclosed distress. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Negotiate a trial of an antidepressant and review his symptom score in four weeks
options.rationale: Medication is an equally effective option at this severity, but he has given a specific and answerable reason for declining, and overriding a clearly stated preference at the first consultation predicts non-adherence and disengagement. Discontinuation symptoms are better addressed as information than as a reason to push the prescription now. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Moderate depression can be treated with structured psychological therapy, an antidepressant, or both, and the evidence does not strongly separate them at this severity, so patient preference legitimately decides. The Australian mechanism for accessing subsidised therapy is a mental health treatment plan prepared by the general practitioner, which gives access to a set number of individual sessions per calendar year with review after the initial block. Telehealth delivered therapy has been shown to be non-inferior to in-person delivery for depression and anxiety and is specifically valuable for rural, remote and rostered workers. Fly in fly out workers carry elevated rates of psychological distress and hazardous drinking, and their rosters are the practical barrier to conventional weekly therapy. Six standard drinks on two or three nights a week exceeds the national guideline of no more than ten standard drinks a week and no more than four on any one day, so it is addressed as part of the plan rather than ignored.
key_points: Structured therapy and antidepressants are comparably effective at moderate severity
A mental health treatment plan is the access route to subsidised sessions
Telehealth delivery is non-inferior and solves the roster problem
Unguided digital programs are for mild, not moderate, depression
His drinking exceeds the national guideline and belongs in the same plan
explanation.pearls: The national alcohol guideline threshold to quote him is no more than ten standard drinks in a week and no more than four on any single day, and his pattern of six drinks in a night breaches the daily limit even though his gamma glutamyl transferase is normal, because that enzyme typically only rises after sustained daily intake rather than intermittent heavy sessions.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners
National Health and Medical Research Council: Australian guidelines to reduce health risks from drinking alcohol
